title: A procedural code, not a policy
paras: Let's start with what this Order is — a procedural code, not a policy. It's the rulebook for how applications are handled in England: validation, publicity, consultation, timing, the decision notice, the register. What it never touches is whether permission should be granted — that's the development plan and national policy. The precise references live in the written guide; I'll keep them out of it.

It's delegated legislation, so it can't go beyond the powers in the primary Act. It replaced an earlier version and has been amended repeatedly. And don't confuse it with its companion, the permitted development order, which grants permission for whole classes of development. This is procedure; that's a grant of rights.

title: Where it sits in the hierarchy
paras: So where does it sit? An application is made under the primary Act, but whether it's validly made and how it's processed is answered almost entirely by this Order and the fees regulations. The Act supplies the substantive powers — form and content, ownership certificates and notice, the power to grant or refuse, the right of appeal, the standard duration of a permission — and the Order puts procedural flesh on them.

It doesn't sit alone. The fees regulations set the fee that must accompany an application, itself an ingredient of validity. The EIA regulations overlay extra procedure on EIA development — screening, scoping, the environmental statement, its own publicity and consultation. The listed buildings regulations run the parallel procedure where heritage's engaged. And national policy, though not part of the Order, shapes how its discretions are exercised.

title: Scope, and the amendment problem
paras: Next, scope — and the amendment problem. It applies to England; Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland run their own systems. The interpretation provision defines major development, which drives the thirteen-week period and much of the publicity and consultation regime. Major means ten or more dwellings; or, where the number's unknown, a site of half a hectare or more; or a thousand square metres or more of floorspace; or a site of a hectare or more — with matching thresholds for minerals and waste.

The amendment problem deserves emphasis. This has been amended so often — the 2018 changes brought in the machinery for consulting on pre-commencement conditions, 2021 adjusted the validation detail, and most recently the 2024 net gain changes threaded through it — that citing it from memory, or an old print-out, is hazardous. The only safe source is the consolidated, in-force version; treat every article number as something to re-confirm.

title: Form and content (article 7)
paras: On to form and content — for any application, outline included. It must be in writing, on the published form — in practice the standard form through the Planning Portal — with the particulars the form requires, a plan identifying the land, and any other plans and drawings needed to describe the development, to a stated scale and showing north.

Since the 2024 net gain changes it must also carry the biodiversity gain information, subject to exemptions — the completed metric calculations, habitat descriptions, and plans identifying on-site and irreplaceable habitat. These are the national requirements: the irreducible content every application needs to be validated anywhere in England. Miss them and it isn't properly made — the authority can decline to validate.

title: National and local validation requirements
paras: That takes us to validation — national and local. Beyond the national requirements, an authority can ask for more through a published local list. But the power's bounded: it can only require information reasonably thought to be a material consideration for that type of application, and the requirement must be reasonable to the scale and nature of the development.

So it can't demand disproportionate or irrelevant material as the price of validation, and the guidance presses authorities to keep local lists proportionate. There's a gap, though — no free-standing right of appeal against a refusal to validate. Your options: supply what's demanded; invite reconsideration against the statutory limits; appeal for non-determination once the period's elapsed, though that risks the Inspectorate disagreeing; or, in a clear case, judicial review.

And it matters because the clock doesn't start until a valid application is received — the date of validity, not submission, is when the period runs. Pre-application engagement is the cheapest way to pin down what's needed.

title: Certificates, notices and design statements
paras: Now certificates, notices and design statements. Because an applicant needn't own the land, every application must carry the right ownership certificate — one where the applicant owns the whole site, others where someone else has an interest — and, where required, notice goes to owners and agricultural tenants. A false certificate is a criminal matter, and a defective or dishonest one can undermine the permission.

A design and access statement is required for major development, for development in a conservation area or affecting the setting of designated heritage assets in the specified circumstances, and for listed building consent. It explains the design principles and how access has been handled, and should be proportionate. Householder and minor applications generally don't need one.

title: Outline permission and reserved matters
paras: Next, outline permission and reserved matters — the two-stage route. Outline permission is granted subject to conditions requiring later approval of the reserved matters — access, appearance, landscaping, layout and scale — with a separate application to approve those. It establishes the principle while deferring the detail, the standard vehicle for larger schemes wanting certainty of principle before full design.

The reserved-matters application isn't a fresh grant — it's approval of details within the outline. It must be made within the statutory time limits, and it can't reopen the principle the outline settled. And don't confuse reserved matters with conditions on a full permission reserving details for later — different mechanisms, though both are discharged through the approval-of-details procedure.

title: Publicity (article 15)
paras: Now publicity — tiered to how sensitive the proposal is, through three methods: a site notice, neighbour notification by letter, and newspaper advertisement.

The fullest publicity — a site notice and a newspaper advert — goes to EIA development with an environmental statement, departures from the development plan, and anything affecting a public right of way, with the longer periods: at least thirty days for EIA, twenty-one for departures and rights of way. Major development needs a newspaper advert plus either a site notice or neighbour notification. Everything else — minor and householder — needs either a site notice or neighbour notification. Across the board it now also goes on the authority's website, and where a listed building or conservation area's engaged the parallel regime adds its own notice requirements.

But publicity confers no veto. Representations count only so far as they raise planning considerations, and their number isn't itself material. What it secures is the opportunity to be heard — hence the fixed fourteen, twenty-one or thirty-day periods.

title: When publicity goes wrong
paras: So what happens when publicity goes wrong? Because it's about fairness, a failure can be fatal — but not automatically. The leading illustration is Gerber. Permission for a large solar farm was granted with inadequate publicity and an arguable EIA failing, and a neighbour who'd known nothing challenged long after the window closed — the panels were already going up. The High Court would extend time and quash; the Court of Appeal reversed, refusing relief because of the claimant's delay and the serious prejudice to a developer who'd built out relying on an apparently valid permission.

The lesson: authorities, get publicity right; objectors, challenge promptly. And a deeper principle runs through the EIA cases — procedural failures aren't all equal. Where one defeats the whole purpose of a mandatory procedure, most starkly not carrying out a required environmental impact assessment, the courts won't excuse it; that's Berkeley. But a technical breach that prejudices no one won't be quashed for its own sake.

title: Consultation (article 18 and Schedule 4)
paras: Now consultation. Before granting permission the authority must consult the specified bodies for the listed categories — the statutory consultees: a highway with the highway authority; a flood-risk area with the Environment Agency and the lead local flood authority; a European site or protected species with Natural England, and so on. It gives notice, can't determine for at least twenty-one days afterwards — longer for EIA — and must take into account any representations within the period.

Consultation isn't required where the authority itself is the consultee, where the consultee's given standing advice for defined categories, or where it's already happened. And where an application's amended, the authority must ask whether the change is big enough that those entitled to be consulted should get a fresh chance to comment. That's the Wheatcroft principle: an amendment can be accepted without a fresh application, provided it doesn't so change the proposal that consultees and objectors lose the chance to comment on what's, in substance, a different scheme.

title: The consequences of a consultation failure
paras: What are the consequences of getting consultation wrong? As with publicity, whether it vitiates the permission turns on prejudice and the nature of the duty. Where the consultee left out is one whose input goes to substance — the Environment Agency on flood risk, Natural England on habitats — and a material consideration wasn't before the decision-maker, the permission's vulnerable.

Where the missing consultee could have added nothing that would have changed the outcome, a court's unlikely to quash. Separately, an authority that's created a legitimate expectation of consultation — say by adopting a Statement of Community Involvement promising to consult a particular way — can be held to it. So these failures turn on whether a real input was lost or a real expectation defeated, not on the breach alone.

title: The time periods (article 34)
paras: Now the time periods for determination, each starting the day after a valid application is received: thirteen weeks for major development, eight weeks for everything else, sixteen weeks for EIA development with an environmental statement, and ten or five weeks for technical details consent following permission in principle.

But a longer period can be agreed in writing between applicant and authority — and that's reshaped practice. Rather than let an application fall to non-determination, the two sides routinely agree an extension, so the statutory period's now a starting point for negotiation more than a hard deadline. It's a maximum, not a target — the authority can decide sooner, but not too soon: it can't determine until the consultation and publicity periods have run. And an extension agreed in writing still counts as in time for the national performance measures.

title: Extensions, PPAs and the planning guarantee
paras: Three related mechanisms sit around that period. The extension of time agreement swaps the statutory period for a longer agreed one. A planning performance agreement — a PPA — is more structured, a project-management contract for larger schemes setting out milestones, resourcing and timescales; not a way to buy a decision, but a framework for delivering one predictably.

The planning guarantee is the backstop. An application, including any appeal, is expected to conclude within twenty-six weeks, and where the authority fails to determine within that overall period the fee is refunded. And authorities that persistently miss the time limits, or whose decisions are overturned on appeal too often, risk designation — which lets applicants in a designated area apply directly to the Secretary of State.

title: Delegation, committee and the officer’s report
paras: Now delegation and committee. The Order fixes the procedure but not where the decision sits inside the authority — that's the scheme of delegation. In practice the great majority, commonly put at around nine in ten, are decided by officers under delegated powers, with only the larger, more contentious or departure applications going to committee.

For a delegated decision the officer's report effectively is the decision — it records the analysis, the consultation responses, the planning balance and the recommendation, and it's what a court scrutinises on challenge. For a committee decision the report advises the members, who decide; where they depart from the recommendation, the reasons must be recorded, because the duty to give reasons can bite. Either way it's the written reasoning that makes a decision defensible.

title: The decision notice and reasons (article 35)
paras: The decision notice itself. Where permission's granted subject to conditions, it must state clearly and precisely the full reasons for each condition — and, for any pre-commencement condition, why it must be discharged before development can begin. Where it's refused, it must give the full reasons, specifying every relevant development-plan policy and proposal. It must also carry a statement of whether and how the authority worked with the applicant positively and proactively, the appeal-rights notification in the prescribed form, and, since 2024, deal with the biodiversity gain condition where permission's granted.

One point of history. Authorities no longer have to give full reasons for a grant — that went in 2013, leaving the duty attached to conditions and refusals. That doesn't mean a grant needs no reasoning; the officer's report supplies it, and a common-law duty to give reasons for a grant still arises in some circumstances. But the notice itself, for an unconditional or lightly conditioned grant, is spare — the reasons that matter for defending it live in the report.

title: Approving details reserved by condition
paras: Once permission's granted, the Order gives you the procedure for approving the details conditions have reserved. An application to approve any matter required by a condition — the everyday discharge-of-conditions application — must be determined within eight weeks, or sixteen for EIA development.

There's also a deemed discharge regime: an applicant who's applied and been met with delay can, after serving the prescribed notice, treat the condition as discharged — unless it's one of the excepted cases. The detail's in the conditions guide. The Order doesn't stop at the grant — it goes on regulating how the permission is worked out through its conditions.

title: Non-determination and appeals
paras: Non-determination and appeals. If the authority doesn't determine within the period — as extended by any written agreement — you can treat the application as refused and appeal; there's a right of appeal against non-determination. The Order and the associated procedure rules run the appeal machinery — the time to lodge, and the written-representations, hearing and inquiry procedures the Planning Inspectorate operates.

A non-determination appeal is tactical: it wrests the decision from a dilatory authority, but it also removes the local decision and your chance to negotiate, and starts a process you can't easily stop. For a straightforward refusal it's the ordinary appeal, the decision notice carrying the appeal-rights notification that starts your time. Appeals against the refusal or non-determination of an approval-of-details application, and against the conditions imposed, run through the same gateway.

title: The register, and life after the decision
paras: Now the register, and life after the decision. Every authority must keep a register of applications — since 2024 also covering biodiversity gain plans — open to public inspection, in two parts. Part one holds applications not yet finally disposed of, with the application, plans and any planning obligations. Part two is the enduring record — decision and conditions, any appeal and outcome, obligations and highways agreements, and now biodiversity gain plans.

It matters beyond the individual application — it's how you establish planning history, evidence a fallback or an extant permission, ground a lawful-development analysis. Entries generally must be made within fourteen days of receipt for a new application. And beyond the register, the standard three-year duration of a permission and the routes for varying one sit outside the Order proper, but complete the life-cycle it begins.

title: Mandatory, directory, and the reluctance to quash
paras: Mandatory versus directory, and the reluctance to quash. The recurring puzzle is whether a requirement is mandatory, so a breach invalidates everything that follows, or merely directory, so substantial compliance suffices. Modern courts have moved away from that rigid split, toward asking what consequence Parliament intended for the failure — and whether it caused substantial prejudice.

So the system takes procedure seriously without being enslaved to it. A failure that deprives someone of a fair chance to take part, or defeats a mandatory assessment, will bite; one that harmed no one usually won't. Three themes. Purpose governs — the more fundamental the procedure to fairness or an EIA obligation, the less willing the court to excuse a breach; that's Berkeley. Prejudice governs relief — even a real breach may not be quashed where no one's prejudiced, and the courts increasingly ask whether the outcome would really have differed. And promptness governs standing — as Gerber shows, delay while a developer builds in good faith can leave even a good point with no remedy. The best practice isn't to generate points to take, but to remove them by getting the process right.

title: The moving parts: reform and currency
paras: Finally, the moving parts — reform and currency. The Order's being reworked around its edges. None of it displaces the architecture we've walked through: an application made and validated, publicised and consulted on, determined within a period that can be extended, the decision notified with reasons for conditions and refusals, and recorded on a public register with appeal on a decision or on time running out.

Three to watch. Biodiversity net gain — the 2024 amendments have threaded net-gain requirements through the form-and-content, decision-notice and register provisions, but the thresholds and exemptions are still settling and should be checked on the file. Statutory consultee reform — from early 2025 the Government's been consulting on a substantial cut to the consultee system, including stripping statutory status from bodies like Sport England, the Theatres Trust and the Gardens Trust; which entries survive needs confirming against the current Order. And the Planning and Infrastructure Act, which got Royal Assent at the end of 2025, carries measures whose commencement and detailed effect were still being worked through secondary legislation. Add the push toward digital planning data and a restructured national policy framework, and the job is to hold the stable structure and the moving detail in the same view.
